2. PRESIDENTIAL REMOVAL POWER AND THE 
CONSTITUTIONALITY OF INDEPENDENT AGENCIES
a. WEat Is Agency ‘Tndependence” and Does It Matter?
Appointments Clause jurisprudence reaffirms that it is the President 
who must appoint all principal officers of the United States and that 
presidential appointment, with Senate advice and consent, is the default 
rule even for inferior officers. The President’s appointment opportunities, 
however, do not necessarily ensure that the administrators who staff the 
executive branch will rehably conform their discretionary initiatives to the 
President’s guidance. For this reason, presidents have long urged that the 
Constitution also guarantees “the chief executive” the power to remove 
officers of the United States and that the power to fire, as well as to hire, 
is indispensable to the uniform execution of the law. Yet the scope of 
presidential removal power remains hotly debated by both jurists and 
scholars well into the Nation’s third century—debated even among the 
authors of your text! The following materials are intended both to 
illuminate current doctrine and the enduring arguments surrounding 
presidential claims to comprehensive removal power.
The issue regarding presidential removal power is often equated with the 
question, “Are the so-called ‘independent agencies’ constitutional?” Such 
agencies, with few exceptions, have been multi-headed boards or commissions 
hke the Federal Election Commission discussed in Buckley v. Valeo, 
Independent agency members are typically appointed to staggered terms of 
specified length (ordinarily longer than four years), and their organic statutes 
provide that no more than a bare majority can represent the same political 
party. What makes such agencies “independent,” however, is that the agency 
heads also enjoy statutory protection against removal except for cause. It is 
conventionally understood that it would not be cause for removal that such an 
administrator declined to follow the President’s poUcy preferences in favor of 
pohcy initiatives that the administrator prefers and which are also within the 
administrator’s lawful discretion. Seila Law LLC v. Consumer Fin. Prot. 
Bureau^ 591 U.S. 197, 229—230 (2020); Peter M. Shane, Independent 
Policymaking and Presidential Power: A Constitutional Analysis, 57 Ge o . 
Wa s h . L. Re v . 596, 608—09 (1989). Yet despite the well-known critical 
characterization of such agencies, quoted earher, as constituting a “headless 
fourth branch of government,” both “executive” and “independent” agencies are 
generally “in” the executive branch, at least if they perform functions 
constitutionally reserved to “officers of the United States.” What distinguishes 
the two sets of agencies is only the degree to which Congress has designed the 
agency to limit the president’s influence over agency pohcy making. Thus, to 
cah the Federal Election Commission “independent” and the Environmental 
Protection Agency “executive” is simply to recognize the statutory difFerences 
that cahbrate presidential power over the agency, not a difference in location 
on a constitutional “organization chart.”
